short_description: A cell — a goat mammary cell, a bacterium or a silkworm cell, depending on the route taken — carrying one or more spider genes so that it manufactures spidroin, the fibre-forming protein spiders spin their thread from. The best-known version is a goat that secretes the protein into its milk; engineered bacteria and silkworms that replace or supplement their usual silk protein with spidroin are the other two routes in active use.

labels.desc: Holds the genome, including the inserted spider silk (spidroin) gene — not visually distinguishable as a single locus.
Ribosomes on its surface synthesize the spidroin chain directly into the ER lumen for folding and initial processing.
Shuttle newly made spidroin from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.
Further processes and sorts the spidroin protein, packaging it into secretory vesicles.
Store the finished, concentrated spidroin protein and carry it to the apical membrane.
Where secretory vesicles fuse and release spidroin protein out of the cell, into the gland lumen.
Supplies the ATP needed for the heavy biosynthetic and secretory workload.
Fills the cell around the nucleus and organelles, housing the secretory-pathway machinery.

do_not_draw: No spider — no legs, arachnid body, spinnerets, or eyes; this is a mammalian (or, for the alternative routes, bacterial/insect) cell, not an animal.

No web, and no finished/spun thread or fibre inside or around the cell — the cell only makes raw soluble protein; spinning it into thread is a separate downstream process, not something the cell itself does.

No visible 'gene' drawn as a discrete glowing/marked object inside the nucleus — DNA in a nucleus is not visually distinguishable locus-by-locus; do not fabricate a highlighted spot, ribbon, or double-helix icon labelled as 'the spider gene'.
No udder or goat anatomy — this is a single cell, not an animal; no fur, hooves, or whole-organ silhouette.
No bacterial cell wall, nucleoid, plasmid ring, or flagellum, unless a render is explicitly and separately built to depict the bacterial-route variant (not the primary depiction for this entry).
No spider spinning-duct anatomy (ampullate gland structures, valve, taper, draw-down zone) borrowed to decorate the cell — that belongs to the spider's own spinning apparatus, a different subject.
No milk fat globules or casein micelles unless a specific render simply and clearly justifies including them as background context — they are not part of the spidroin secretory story.
No baked-in text, letters, numbers, scale bars, or watermarks; no black border/frame/vignette/letterbox.

reference_candidates.attribution: Louisa Howard, Dartmouth Electron Microscope Facility (JEOL 100CX TEM)
reference_candidates.shows: TEM of a mammalian pancreatic acinar cell: nucleus, mitochondria, rough endoplasmic reticulum, and zymogen (secretory) granules. Not mammary tissue and not a transgenic cell — used as the best available free-licensed structural analog of the same category of cell (a polarized, protein-secreting exocrine glandular epithelial cell using the RER → Golgi → secretory-granule → apical-exocytosis pathway a spider-silk-producing mammary cell also uses). Must be captioned explicitly as an analog, not verified mammary or transgenic tissue.

reference_candidates.shows: Mouse-tissue TEM showing both rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Generic ER reference, no secretory granules/vesicles visible, cell type/tissue of origin not specified beyond 'mouse tissue' — lower priority than ranks 1-2 but a confirmed, more permissively licensed fallback.

Option (b) fallback (spider silk gland/duct anatomy) was searched but no freely-licensed photographic micrograph was found — only vector schematic diagrams exist on Wikimedia Commons (e.g. File:Spider silk duct.svg, Category:Spider silk), which are diagrams, not real microscopy, so they do not satisfy the 'real microscopy' requirement. A genuine mammary-specific secretory-cell TEM was found in the literature (Honvo-Houéto et al. 2016, Molecular Biology of the Cell 27(19):2946-2964, showing ER and casein-containing secretory vesicles near the apical membrane) but is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (NonCommercial) and is therefore excluded. Suggested further queries for a later fetch step: 'site:commons.wikimedia.org mammary gland electron micrograph', 'NCBI Bookshelf mammary alveolar cell TEM public domain', 'PMC open access mammary epithelial cell TEM rough endoplasmic reticulum CC BY' (filter out CC BY-NC/CC BY-NC-SA results), and NIAID/NIH Flickr (flickr.com/photos/niaid) for any public-domain mammary-tissue EM plates.
